claim: AAV-eGFP expression in striatum of ChAT-Cre mice is highly specific, with 95.9 ± 0.78% colocalization with choline acetyltransferase immunostaining.
source: The eGFP expression in striatum of ChAT-Cre and PV-Cre mice was highly specific as demonstrated by colocalization with immunohistochemical staining for choline acetyltransferase or parvalbumin (Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c, ChAT 95.9 ± 0.78%, PV 95.6 ± 0.79%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization data from immunohistochemical experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: AAV-eGFP expression in striatum of PV-Cre mice is highly specific, with 95.6 ± 0.79% colocalization with parvalbumin immunostaining.
source: The eGFP expression in striatum of ChAT-Cre and PV-Cre mice was highly specific as demonstrated by colocalization with immunohistochemical staining for choline acetyltransferase or parvalbumin (Figure 1a,b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c, ChAT 95.9 ± 0.78%, PV 95.6 ± 0.79%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization data from immunohistochemical experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: ChAT interneurons are tonically active.
source: ChAT interneurons are tonically active, have depolarized resting membrane potentials, and feature prominent hyperpolarization-activation cation currents (Figure 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiological recordings showing tonic activity in ChAT interneurons.

claim: ChAT interneurons have depolarized resting membrane potentials.
source: ChAT interneurons are tonically active, have depolarized resting membrane potentials, and feature prominent hyperpolarization-activation cation currents (Figure 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiological recordings from ChAT interneurons.

claim: ChAT interneurons feature prominent hyperpolarization-activation cation currents.
source: ChAT interneurons are tonically active, have depolarized resting membrane potentials, and feature prominent hyperpolarization-activation cation currents (Figure 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo electrophysiological recordings showing characteristic currents in ChAT interneurons.

claim: PV interneurons exhibit narrow action potentials.
source: while PV interneurons exhibit narrow action potentials and high firing rates (Gittis et al., 2010; Tepper et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and cited literature.

claim: PV interneurons exhibit high firing rates.
source: while PV interneurons exhibit narrow action potentials and high firing rates (Gittis et al., 2010; Tepper et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and cited literature.

claim: There was no significant difference in the total number of input neurons for ChAT and PV interneurons (ChAT 6580 ± 2657, PV 4456 ± 1540; two-tailed t-test, p=0.4773).
source: There was no significant difference in the total number of input neurons for ChAT and PV interneurons (ChAT 6580 ± 2657, PV 4456 ± 1540; two-tailed t-test, p=0.4773).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of rabies tracing data with statistical testing.

claim: Both ChAT and PV interneurons received a vast majority of inputs from the cortex.
source: The tracing results revealed that both types of striatal interneurons received a vast majority of inputs from the cortex (Figure 2b, two-way ANOVA, F (3, 36)=325.1, p<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative rabies tracing data analyzed with two-way ANOVA.

claim: ChAT interneurons received significantly more inputs from layer five compared to all other cortical layers.
source: ChAT interneurons received significantly more inputs from layer five compared to all other cortical layers and more layer 2/3 compared to layer six projections (Figure 2c; two-way ANOVA, Sidak's, 5 vs. 6, p<0.0001; 2/3 vs. 6, p=0.0019; 2/3 vs. 5, p=0.0041).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cortical layer distribution with statistical testing.

claim: ChAT interneurons received significantly more inputs from associative than sensorimotor cortex.
source: ChAT interneurons received significantly more inputs from associative than sensorimotor cortex (Figure 2d, two-way ANOVA, Sidak's multiple comparisons test, p=0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cortical inputs categorized by functional region with statistical testing.

claim: Association cortex inputs to ChAT interneurons were layer 2/3 dominant with significantly more layer 2/3 inputs than layer six and more layer five inputs than layer 6.
source: Association cortex inputs to ChAT interneurons were layer 2/3 dominant with significantly more layer 2/3 inputs than layer six and more layer five inputs than layer 6 (Figure 2e; two-way ANOVA, Sidak's, layer 2/3 vs. 6, p<0.0001, layer 5 vs. 6, p=0.0012).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laminar distribution in association cortex with statistical testing.

claim: PV interneurons association cortical inputs were more layer 2/3 preferring.
source: Similarly, PV interneurons association cortical inputs were more layer 2/3 preferring (Figure 2e; two-way ANOVA, Sidak's, layer 2/3 vs. 6, p<0.0001, layer 2/3 vs 5, p=0.0029).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laminar distribution in association cortex with statistical testing.

claim: Sensorimotor inputs to ChAT interneurons originated predominately from layer 5.
source: Sensorimotor inputs to ChAT interneurons originated predominately from layer 5 (Figure 2f; two-way ANOVA, Sidak's, layer 5 vs. 6, p=0.0010, layer 2/3 vs. 5, p=0.0086.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laminar distribution in sensorimotor cortex with statistical testing.

claim: PV interneurons received significantly more sensorimotor layer 5 than layer 2/3 projections.
source: PV interneurons also received significantly more sensorimotor layer 5 than layer 2/3 projections (Figure 2f; two-way ANOVA, Sidak's, layer 2/3 vs. 5, p=0.0018).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of laminar distribution in sensorimotor cortex with statistical testing.

claim: PV interneurons receive a projection from the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN).
source: Our dG-rabies tracing surprisingly revealed that PV interneurons receive a projection from the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) (Figure 2a, Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by rabies tracing data showing labeled neurons in TRN projecting to PV interneurons.

claim: The rabies-eGFP signal in TRN colocalized with parvalbumin (PV) immunostaining at 33.44 ± 6.08%.
source: The rabies-eGFP signal was clearly located within the TRN as evidenced by colocalization with parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SOM) immunostaining (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017) (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f, PV: rabies-eGFP colocalization 33.44 ± 6.08%, SOM: rabies-eGFP colocalization 43.73 ± 3.88%)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis of rabies-labeled neurons with immunohistochemical markers.

claim: The rabies-eGFP signal in TRN colocalized with somatostatin (SOM) immunostaining at 43.73 ± 3.88%.
source: The rabies-eGFP signal was clearly located within the TRN as evidenced by colocalization with parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SOM) immunostaining (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017) (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f, PV: rabies-eGFP colocalization 33.44 ± 6.08%, SOM: rabies-eGFP colocalization 43.73 ± 3.88%)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis of rabies-labeled neurons with immunohistochemical markers.

claim: Brief paired blue laser stimulation of TRN ChR2-positive terminals in the striatum exhibited fast latency, monosynaptic IPSCs in 53.8% (7/13) of PV interneurons recorded.
source: Brief paired blue laser stimulation of TRN ChR2-positive terminals in the striatum over PV interneurons, in the presence of AMPAR and NMDAR antagonists, exhibited fast latency, monosynaptic IPSCs in 53.8% (7/13) of the cells recorded (Figure 3h–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: TRN-evoked IPSCs in PV interneurons were blocked by the GABAAR antagonist picrotoxin.
source: These large, reliable, and paired-pulse depressing IPSCs were blocked by the GABAAR antagonist picrotoxin (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing blockade of IPSCs with picrotoxin.

claim: Neighboring PV-negative cells (putative SPNs) exhibited no functional connectivity with TRN terminals (0/8 cells).
source: In order to test the selectivity of this input, neighboring PV-negative cells (putative SPNs) were also recorded, yet none of these neurons exhibited any functional connectivity (0/8 cells) (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell recordings from neighboring non-PV neurons showing absence of connectivity.

claim: One second constant blue laser stimulation of TRN axon terminals was sufficient to suppress current injection-evoked spiking in PV interneurons.
source: In current clamp, one second constant blue laser stimulation of TRN axon terminals was sufficient to suppress current injection-evoked spiking in PV interneurons (Figure 3k).
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings showing suppression of spiking during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Approximately 40% (83/205) of putative SPNs showed light-induced firing rate modulation during TRN terminal stimulation.
source: Of the over two hundred putative SPNs recorded, around 40% show a firing rate change during light stimulation (83/205).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Half of the responsive SPN population (44/83) exhibited delayed inhibition during TRN terminal stimulation.
source: Noticeably, half of the responsive SPN population (44/83) exhibited delayed inhibition during the one second constant laser stimulation (Figure 3m,o)
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings showing delayed inhibition in a subset of SPNs.

claim: 39/83 responsive SPNs exhibited slow latency excitation during TRN terminal stimulation.
source: while others (39/83) exhibited slow latency excitation (Figure 3n,o).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings showing excitation in a subset of SPNs.

claim: Four putative striatal PV interneurons (fast-spiking interneurons) were identified in in vivo recordings and all of them show inhibited firing activity during TRN terminal stimulation.
source: Indeed, four putative striatal PV interneurons (fast-spiking interneurons) were identified in our recordings and all of them show inhibited firing activity during TRN terminal stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings from putative PV interneurons during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: GPe was the most predominant basal ganglia input to both ChAT and PV interneurons.
source: Rabies tracing revealed that all basal ganglia nuclei similarly innervate both ChAT and PV interneurons, and of these basal ganglia inputs, GPe was the most predominant (two-way ANOVA, F (6, 63)=27.27, p<0.0001, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative rabies tracing data analyzed with two-way ANOVA.

claim: Few rabies-eGFP GPe neurons colocalized with PV immunostaining (ChAT-projecting: 3.5%, PV-projecting: 2.8%).
source: and few rabies-eGFP GPe neurons were colocalized with either PV immmunostaining (ChAT-projecting: 3.5%, PV-projecting: 2.8%; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–e)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis of rabies-labeled GPe neurons with immunohistochemical markers.

claim: Few rabies-eGFP GPe neurons colocalized with ChAT immunostaining (ChAT-projecting: 1.6%, PV-projecting: 1.3%).
source: or ChAT immmunostaining (ChAT-projecting: 1.6%, PV-projecting: 1.3%; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis of rabies-labeled GPe neurons with immunohistochemical markers.

claim: Fast latency, monosynaptic IPSCs were observed in both ChAT-positive (11/11) and ChAT-negative neurons (putative SPNs, 7/7) following GPe terminal stimulation.
source: Fast latency, monosynaptic IPSCs were observed in both ChAT-positive (11/11) and ChAT-negative neurons (putative SPNs, 7/7) (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings with optogenetic stimulation of GPe terminals.

claim: GPe-evoked IPSCs were confirmed by blockade with the GABAAR antagonist picrotoxin.
source: These IPSCs were confirmed by blockade with the GABAAR antagonist picrotoxin (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments showing blockade of IPSCs with picrotoxin.

claim: PV interneurons exhibited larger IPSCs than neighboring SPNs following GPe terminal stimulation (two-tailed t-test, p<0.0001).
source: Recordings from pairs of PV interneurons and neighboring SPNs revealed that PV interneurons exhibited larger IPSCs (two-tailed t-test, p<0.0001), higher release probability (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0114), and greater 1/(CV)^2 (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0277) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2e–g)
evidence: The claim is supported by paired recordings comparing IPSC amplitudes with statistical testing.

claim: PV interneurons exhibited higher release probability than neighboring SPNs following GPe terminal stimulation (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0114).
source: Recordings from pairs of PV interneurons and neighboring SPNs revealed that PV interneurons exhibited larger IPSCs (two-tailed t-test, p<0.0001), higher release probability (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0114), and greater 1/(CV)^2 (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0277) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2e–g)
evidence: The claim is supported by paired recordings comparing release probability with statistical testing.

claim: PV interneurons exhibited greater 1/(CV)^2 than neighboring SPNs following GPe terminal stimulation (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0277).
source: Recordings from pairs of PV interneurons and neighboring SPNs revealed that PV interneurons exhibited larger IPSCs (two-tailed t-test, p<0.0001), higher release probability (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0114), and greater 1/(CV)^2 (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0277) (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2e–g)
evidence: The claim is supported by paired recordings comparing trial-to-trial variance with statistical testing.

claim: The ChAT to SPN IPSC ratio was lower than the PV to SPN ratio (Mann Whitney test, p=0.0076).
source: Overall, the ChAT to SPN IPSC ratio was lower than the PV to SPN ratio, suggesting increased functional connectivity from GPe to PV compared to ChAT interneurons, despite similar numbers of GPe neurons projecting to both (Figure 4c, Mann Whitney test, p=0.0076).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of IPSC ratios with statistical testing.

claim: GPe terminal stimulation significantly reduced tonic firing in ChAT interneurons (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0043).
source: Interleaved blue laser light stimulation of GPe inhibitory terminals on ChAT interneurons was sufficient to significantly reduce tonic firing (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 2h–j, two-tailed t-test, p=0.0043).
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings showing reduced firing during optogenetic stimulation with statistical testing.

claim: After cessation of GPe terminal stimulation, ChAT neurons showed significant rebound activity spiking at rates above baseline (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0469).
source: After cessation of laser stimulation, ChAT neurons showed significant rebound activity spiking at rates above baseline (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 2h–j, two-tailed t-test, p=0.0469).
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings showing rebound activity after stimulation with statistical testing.

claim: Inhibitory inputs from GPe were sufficient to inhibit current injection-induced spiking in PV interneurons for a few hundred milliseconds following blue laser stimulation (two-tailed t-test, p=0.0401).
source: Furthermore, inhibitory inputs from GPe were sufficient to inhibit current injection-induced spiking in PV interneurons for a few hundred milliseconds following blue laser stimulation (Figure 4f,g; Figure 4—figure supplement 2k,l; two-tailed t-test, p=0.0401).
evidence: The claim is supported by current clamp recordings showing suppression of spiking with statistical testing.

claim: Of all the SPNs responsive to GPe terminal stimulation (22/81), the majority showed inhibited firing activity (16/22) while a small proportion was excited (6/22).
source: It revealed that of all the SPNs responsive to GPe terminal stimulation (22/81), the majority showed inhibited firing activity (16/22) while a small proportion was excited (6/22) (Figure 4i–k).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo extracellular recordings with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: No overlap in immunostaining for ChAT and eGFP rabies-labeled neurons in the PPN was observed.
source: However, no overlap in immunostaining for ChAT and eGFP rabies-labeled neurons in the PPN was observed (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical analysis showing lack of colocalization.

claim: eGFP axon terminal expression from PPN in the striatum was sparse and directed, wrapping the cell somas and proximal dendrites of ChAT interneurons.
source: Interestingly, while the eGFP axon terminal expression in the striatum was sparse, it was directed, wrapping the cell somas and proximal dendrites of ChAT interneurons (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical tracing showing terminal distribution patterns.

claim: ChAT interneurons exhibited fast latency, monosynaptic (<6 ms), excitatory currents in a vast majority of neurons sampled (10/11).
source: ChAT interneurons exhibited fast latency, monosynaptic (<6 ms), excitatory currents in a vast majority of neurons sampled (10/11), while only a few neighboring SPNs (3/25) exhibited fast latency (<6 ms), excitatory or inhibitory connections (Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings with optogenetic stimulation of PPN terminals.

claim: Only a few neighboring SPNs (3/25) exhibited fast latency (<6 ms), excitatory or inhibitory connections from PPN.
source: ChAT interneurons exhibited fast latency, monosynaptic (<6 ms), excitatory currents in a vast majority of neurons sampled (10/11), while only a few neighboring SPNs (3/25) exhibited fast latency (<6 ms), excitatory or inhibitory connections (Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell voltage clamp recordings showing low connectivity to SPNs.

claim: The striatum is primarily composed of spiny projection neurons (SPNs), which consist of ~95% of total striatal neuronal population.
source: The striatum is primarily composed of spiny projection neurons (SPNs), which consist of ~95% of total striatal neuronal population (Gerfen et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on striatal cell composition.

claim: ChAT interneurons account for only 1–2% of the total striatal population.
source: While ChAT interneurons account for only 1–2% of the total striatal population, the striatum contains some of the highest levels of cholinergic markers in the brain.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about striatal cell type composition.

claim: The striatum contains some of the highest levels of cholinergic markers in the brain.
source: While ChAT interneurons account for only 1–2% of the total striatal population, the striatum contains some of the highest levels of cholinergic markers in the brain.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cholinergic marker distribution in the brain.

claim: Dysfunction of striatal ChAT interneurons has been implicated in numerous psychiatric disorders including schizophrenia, depression, and other mood disorders.
source: Dysfunction of striatal ChAT interneurons has been implicated in numerous psychiatric disorders including schizophrenia, depression, and other mood disorders (Scarr et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on ChAT interneuron dysfunction in psychiatric disorders.

claim: ChAT interneurons exhibit a pause and subsequent rebound firing in response to the presentation of a cue predictive of reward or aversion.
source: ChAT interneurons are tonically active and exhibit a pause and subsequent rebound firing in response to the presentation of a cue predictive of reward or aversion (Ding et al., 2010; English et al., 2012; Kimura et al., 1984; Schulz and Reynolds, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on ChAT interneuron firing patterns during behavior.

claim: The conditioned pause in ChAT interneurons is thought to encode the salience of external stimuli supporting the association of cue with action or outcome.
source: This conditioned pause is thought to encode the salience of external stimuli supporting the association of cue with action or outcome (Aosaki et al., 1994; Kimura et al., 1984; Ravel et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature proposing a functional role for the pause response.

claim: A vast majority of excitatory inputs to ChAT interneurons are thought to originate from centromedian and parafascicular nuclei of the thalamus.
source: A vast majority of excitatory inputs to ChAT interneurons are thought to originate from centromedian and parafascicular nuclei of the thalamus (Ding et al., 2010; Lapper and Bolam, 1992)
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on thalamic inputs to ChAT interneurons.

claim: Cortical stimulation has been shown to increase ChAT interneuron firing.
source: however, cortical stimulation has been shown to increase ChAT interneuron firing as well (Ding et al., 2010), suggesting a wealth of underappreciated cortical inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on cortical effects on ChAT interneuron activity.

claim: PV interneurons constitute ~1% of the total striatal neuronal population.
source: PV interneurons (also known as fast-spiking interneurons) constitute ~1% of the total striatal neuronal population
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about striatal cell type composition.

claim: PV interneuron dysfunction has been implicated in multiple movement disorders and neuropsychiatric disorders including Huntington's disease, dystonia, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and Tourette's syndrome (TS).
source: and their dysfunction has been implicated in multiple movement disorders and neuropsychiatric disorders including Huntington's disease, dystonia, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and Tourette's syndrome (TS) (Burguière et al., 2015; Kalanithi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on PV interneuron dysfunction in neurological disorders.

claim: PV interneurons are capable of firing at very high rates in vitro and in vivo.
source: These neurons are capable of firing at very high rates in vitro and in vivo (Gage et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on PV interneuron firing properties.

claim: PV interneurons provide strong feedforward inhibition onto SPNs.
source: providing strong feedforward inhibition onto SPNs (Gittis et al., 2010; Koós and Tepper, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on PV interneuron connectivity and function.

claim: Striatal PV interneurons are believed to receive inputs primarily from cortex and globus pallidus, with minimal thalamic innervation.
source: Striatal PV interneurons are believed to receive inputs primarily from cortex and globus pallidus, with minimal thalamic innervation (Bevan et al., 1998; Mallet et al., 2012; Saunders et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on inputs to PV interneurons.

claim: The TRN is a thin shell of GABAergic neurons that was thought to project within thalamus regulating thalamocortical and corticothalamic communications.
source: The TRN is a thin shell of GABAergic neurons that was thought to project within thalamus regulating thalamocortical and corticothalamic communications (Halassa and Acsády, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on TRN anatomy and function.

claim: The TRN to striatal PV interneuron pathway represents a substantial and selective inhibitory input to striatal PV interneurons as this pathway has not been observed in previous rabies tracing datasets on other striatal cell types.
source: This projection represents a substantial and selective inhibitory input to striatal PV interneurons as this pathway has not been observed in previous rabies tracing datasets on other striatal cell types (Guo et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with cited literature showing absence of this pathway in other cell types.

claim: GPe primarily targets PV interneurons and SPNs.
source: Previous studies have suggested that GPe primarily targets PV interneurons and SPNs (Bevan et al., 1998; Gittis et al., 2014; Mallet et al., 2012; Saunders et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on GPe connectivity.

claim: There is anatomical evidence of a GPe projection to ChAT interneurons.
source: along with evidence of an anatomical connection to ChAT interneurons (Guo et al., 2015; Mallet et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature showing anatomical evidence of GPe to ChAT connectivity.

claim: Striatum-projecting GPe neurons play a crucial role during action cancelling.
source: Considering recent studies implying that striatum-projecting GPe neurons play a crucial role during action cancelling (Mallet et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on GPe function in behavior.

claim: Previous literature suggested a significant anatomical cholinergic PPN input to striatum.
source: Previous literature suggested a significant anatomical cholinergic PPN input to striatum (Dautan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on PPN projections to striatum.

claim: A vast majority of cholinergic neurons in PPN lack expression of vGluT2 mRNA.
source: Yet, previous evidence does not lend strong support for the idea of co-release with a vast majority of cholinergic neurons in PPN lacking expression of vGluT2 mRNA (Wang and Morales, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature on neurotransmitter expression in PPN neurons.

claim: Several striatal rabies tracing studies do not find significant rabies labeling of dopamine neurons in the substania nigra pars compacta (SNc), despite the dense innervation of dopamine terminals from the SNc in dorsal striatum.
source: For example, several striatal rabies tracing studies using the same technique do not find significant rabies labeling of dopamine neurons in the substania nigra pars compacta (SNc) (Smith et al., 2016; Wall et al., 2013), despite the dense innervation of dopamine terminals from the SNc in dorsal striatum.
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature showing limitations of rabies tracing for certain neurotransmitter systems.

claim: ChAT interneurons may receive internal cognitive or external environmental information for context-dependent action modulation.
source: These preferential inputs suggest a potential functional distinction for their role in controlling behavior, whereby ChAT interneurons may receive internal cognitive or external environmental information for context-dependent action modulation
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of associative cortical and thalamic inputs to ChAT interneurons.

claim: PV interneurons may integrate sensorimotor information for action learning and selection.
source: while PV interneurons may integrate sensorimotor information for action learning and selection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of sensorimotor cortical inputs to PV interneurons.

claim: The TRN-striatal PV interneuron pathway could relay attention-related information directly to the striatum.
source: This subcortical pathway is well positioned to relay attention-related information directly to the striatum.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the known role of TRN in attention and its newly discovered projection to striatal PV interneurons.

claim: By targeting striatal PV interneurons, the TRN pathway might be possible to effectively bias action selection and coordinate an animal's ongoing behavior with corresponding attentional state.
source: By targeting striatal PV interneurons, we speculate that it might be possible to effectively bias action selection and coordinate an animal's ongoing behavior with corresponding attentional state (Berke, 2011; Gage et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for the TRN-PV pathway based on cited literature on PV interneuron function.

claim: The TRN-striatal PV interneuron pathway could serve as a subcortical bridge for promptly coordinating sensory attention and actions.
source: Potentially, this pathway could serve as a subcortical bridge for promptly coordinating sensory attention and actions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for the TRN-PV pathway.

claim: The GPe to striatal interneuron projections may be an important part of the feedback circuitry involved in context-dependent action control.
source: our current results thus further reinforce that the GPe to striatal interneuron projections may be an important part of the feedback circuitry involved in context-dependent action control.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional connectivity data and cited literature on GPe function.

claim: ChAT interneurons may not receive direct cholinergic projections from PPN.
source: Alternatively, ChAT interneurons may not receive direct cholinergic projections from PPN.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the lack of colocalization between rabies-labeled PPN neurons and ChAT immunostaining.

claim: Each cell type in the striatum appears to have access to the same inputs within a topographic domain, but significant preferences do exist for certain cell types, which imbues functional distinctions.
source: When our current data are considered collectively with previous studies using monosynaptic rabies tracing from other striatal cell types (Smith et al., 2016; Wall et al., 2013), a general theme appears. Each cell type in the striatum appears to have access to the same inputs within a topographic domain (Hintiryan et al., 2016), but significant preferences do exist for certain cell types, which imbues functional distinctions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of current data with cited literature on other striatal cell types.

claim: The laminar organization of cortical inputs (superficial layer projections from associative cortex versus deep layer projections from sensorimotor cortex) may be a general organizing principle of the cortical inputs to the dorsal striatum.
source: This laminar organization may be a general organizing principle of the cortical inputs to the dorsal striatum.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed pattern in both ChAT and PV tracing data and comparison with cited literature on patch/matrix neurons.

claim: Disinhibition of SPNs via TRN inhibition of striatal PV interneurons may contribute to the firing modulation observed in SPNs during TRN terminal stimulation.
source: While the firing modulation observed in SPNs represents the net network effects of TRN stimulation on basal ganglia output, potential disinhibition of SPNs via TRN inhibition of striatal PV interneurons may contribute to some of these effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed effects on SPNs and the known inhibitory connectivity from TRN to PV interneurons.

claim: GPe inhibitory presynaptic release and/or number of synapses is greater on PV interneurons than on SPNs.
source: suggesting GPe inhibitory presynaptic release and/or number of synapses is greater on PV interneurons than on SPNs (Bevan et al., 1998; Gittis et al., 2014; Glajch et al., 2016; Mallet et al., 2012; Saunders et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in IPSC properties and cited literature on GPe connectivity.

claim: The increased functional connectivity from GPe to PV compared to ChAT interneurons is suggested despite similar numbers of GPe neurons projecting to both.
source: Overall, the ChAT to SPN IPSC ratio was lower than the PV to SPN ratio, suggesting increased functional connectivity from GPe to PV compared to ChAT interneurons, despite similar numbers of GPe neurons projecting to both (Figure 4c, Mann Whitney test, p=0.0076).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of IPSC ratios despite similar anatomical input numbers.

claim: PPN sends a non-cholinergic projection to striatum that preferentially targets ChAT interneurons.
source: Overall these data suggest that PPN sends a non-cholinergic projection to striatum that preferentially targets ChAT interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of ChAT colocalization in rabies-labeled PPN neurons and the preferential connectivity to ChAT interneurons.

claim: ChAT interneurons receive strong functional excitatory inputs on the soma and proximal dendrites from PPN.
source: Overall, these results suggest that different from SPNs, ChAT interneurons receive strong functional excitatory inputs on the soma and proximal dendrites from PPN.
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical tracing showing terminal distribution and electrophysiological recordings showing excitatory currents.
